content:
A violent overnight storm tore through the small Brazilian town of Tupanciretã on Friday, killing three people, injuring at least 60 and ripping the roofs off thousands of homes in less than an hour, according to state authorities in Rio Grande do Sul. The storm struck at around 3 a.m. local time, battering the municipality of about 20,000 people with winds of 114 kilometres per hour, hail and driving rain, and it left the entire town without electricity or running water.

State civil defence officials confirmed the three deaths on Friday morning, and a fourth possible death was under investigation by the afternoon, according to Folha de S.Paulo. The number of injured was still being counted, but local media reported at least 60 people hurt, many of them taken to hospitals in the nearby cities of Santa Maria and Júlio de Castilhos after Tupanciretã's own hospital was badly damaged.

The scale of the destruction is still disputed, and the gap between the figures tells its own story about a town overwhelmed in minutes. The state civil defence agency's first official bulletin put the damage at about 5,000 homes, along with the town's hospital. But Mayor Gustavo Herter Terra put it far higher, estimating that some 8,000 of the municipality's roughly 8,600 houses had been damaged, unroofed or knocked down. "It's something never seen before, a movie scene," the mayor told local media. "Our hospital was blocked by the trees around it, the access roads to the municipality were blocked with trees. The city is finished."

The hospital's roof was destroyed and 11 patients had to be transferred elsewhere, while the building lost its X-ray and ultrasound equipment, according to local reports. Around 100 trees were torn up across the town, and falling debris blocked the roads in and out of the municipality, slowing the first rescue efforts. Emergency crews spent the morning searching the wreckage for more casualties, and officials warned that the toll could still rise.

What exactly hit Tupanciretã is still being established, and that uncertainty matters for how the damage is understood. Civil defence described the storm as a "supercell", a rotating thunderstorm that often precedes a tornado, and its monitoring centre said analysis of images and video pointed to a microburst — a sudden, violent downdraft — within the supercell. Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology recorded winds of 114 kilometres per hour. A tornado has still not been confirmed, and officials said one cannot yet be ruled out, but they added that a tornado alone would not explain the sheer extent of the damage across the town.

One of the deadliest moments came at a party venue in the municipality, where the roof of the structure collapsed during the storm. "We know there was a party in the municipality where the roof of that structure ended up collapsing," Luciano Boeira, the state coordinator of civil defence, told Radio Gaúcha. The identities and circumstances of the three victims had not been officially released by Friday evening.

The storm was not confined to Tupanciretã. Another 32 municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul also reported damage, according to the state government, and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ordered emergency teams to be sent to the region. Governor Eduardo Leite ordered what he called a full-force mobilisation of the state government, and the state allocated 2 million reais, about $330,000, in immediate aid for machinery and emergency equipment, according to [Firstpost](https://www.firstpost.com/world/severe-storm-wreaks-havoc-in-brazil-kills-3-destroys-thousands-of-homes-14061644.html).

Southern Brazil is frequently hit by tornadoes, and Rio Grande do Sul is no stranger to extreme weather. The state was devastated by catastrophic flooding in May 2024 that killed more than 180 people and displaced hundreds of thousands, and its towns have spent the two years since rebuilding homes and infrastructure. Friday's storm is a reminder that the danger in the region does not come only from rising rivers. A supercell can form, strike and vanish in under an hour, leaving a town that was intact at 3 a.m. in ruins before dawn.

For the residents of Tupanciretã, the immediate task is shelter, power and water. With the hospital damaged, roads blocked and thousands of homes unroofed, the state government said rescue and relief teams would remain in the town through the weekend, and officials have not ruled out further casualties being found in the wreckage. The full cost of the storm — in lives, homes and the town's already fragile infrastructure — will only become clear once the counting is done. For now, the town that the mayor described as "finished" faces a long rebuild, and the question of whether a tornado touched down, or a microburst did the damage alone, is one meteorologists will be working to answer in the days ahead, as [Free Malaysia Today](https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/world/2026/11/21/severe-storm-destroys-thousands-of-homes-kills-3-in-brazil) reported.

Natural disasters have struck across the world in recent weeks, from the [magnitude 6.6 earthquake off Indonesia's Tual islands](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/indonesia-earthquake-tual-magnitude-6-6-november-2026) to the [suspected gas explosion in Tbilisi that killed six people](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/tbilisi-gas-explosion-six-killed-ponichala-november-2026). But few have unfolded as fast as the storm over Tupanciretã, where a single hour of wind and hail undid years of rebuilding in a town of 20,000 people.
summary: A violent overnight storm with winds of 114 km/h tore through Tupanciretã in southern Brazil on Friday, killing three people, injuring at least 60 and damaging as many as 8,000 of the town's 8,600 homes, leaving the entire municipality without power or water as rescue teams searched the wreckage.
title: Severe storm kills three and wrecks thousands of homes in southern Brazil town
